# Turn Indicators Don't Work but Hazards Work Fine

This specific failure modeâwhere sequential turn signals fail but simultaneous hazard lights function correctlyâis a classic symptom of a relay or fuse issue, rather than a simple bulb or bulb socket failure. The fact that your hazards work confirms the power source and the ground path for the indicator circuit are intact. If the bulbs themselves were burnt out on both sides simultaneously, or if the wiring harness was severed, the hazard function would also be dead because it relies on the same filaments to light up when the relay is switched to the "hazard" position.

The distinction between left and right indicators failing sequentially points toward a progression in the fault path. In your 2011 Renault Clio, the logic likely follows this sequence: yesterday, the left circuit failed; today, the right joined it. The most probable culprit is the turn signal relay itself or a shared fuse that has degraded. However, the behavior regarding your headlights reveals a more nuanced electrical interaction.

When you engage the right indicator, the headlights illuminate. This is an intentional design feature known as "pilot light" functionality or side marker activation in certain configurations, but the fact that it happens asymmetrically suggests a voltage drop issue on the left side. When the system detects a high resistance or open circuit on the left turn signal line (because the bulb isn't completing the circuit properly), the vehicle's logic may be misinterpreting the load. More likely, the "flasher" module is seeing an imbalance. In many European cars of this era, if one side of the indicator circuit has significantly higher resistanceâperhaps due to a corroded socket or a partially blown filamentâthe flasher unit compensates by dimming the other side or engaging auxiliary lights to maintain symmetry, though your Clio seems to be driving headlight filaments directly in response.

The critical observation is that turning off the left indicator turns off those headlights. This implies a shared control line or a logic gate within the switch assembly where the "off" state of the left signal breaks the circuit powering the headlights, while the "on" state of the right signal activates them. If you were to swap the turn signal bulbs with high-quality OEM replacements and clean the sockets, you might find that the filaments are unevenly burning out due to voltage spikes caused by poor grounding in the dashboard cluster.

From a systems engineering perspective, this behaves like a load-balancing algorithm failing because one node (the left bulb) presents infinite resistance. The flasher relay is designed to detect an open circuit on one side and either blink faster or dim the opposite side. In your case, it appears the system is defaulting to powering the headlights instead of maintaining the hazard state when the imbalance shifts.

To diagnose this without a multimeter, you can check the fuse box under the hood. Look for the specific fuses labeled "Indicator" and "Hazard." Often, these are separate in modern architecture, but on older models like the Clio, they might share a single 10A or 15A fuse that is partially blown (high resistance) rather than completely open. A partially blown fuse will allow current to pass for the low-resistance hazard load but fail under the specific timing requirements of the sequential turn signal relay, causing it to overheat and eventually stop flashing.

If replacing fuses does not resolve the issue, the flasher unit located near the steering column or in the engine bay is likely the point of failure. It is a mechanical electromechanical device that vibrates via a bimetallic strip; if the contacts are pitted or the spring tension has weakened over 13 years, it will fail to switch rapidly enough for sequential lights but might still toggle once for hazards. Replacing this unit is a cheap and effective fix that restores the correct load balancing logic.

For developers building embedded systems with similar redundancy requirements, this scenario illustrates the importance of distinguishing between "circuit open" (no power) and "load mismatch" (power present but incorrect timing). The system should be robust enough to handle asymmetric failures without triggering unintended side effects like headlight activation unless explicitly programmed for safety.
